notes.meaning: Exodus begins by linking directly back to Genesis. It names the sons of Jacob who moved down to Egypt, each bringing his entire household of family and servants. God was already laying the groundwork to turn this single extended family into a mighty nation.

The sons of Jacob are listed according to their mothers, beginning with Leah and Rachel before naming the sons born to the servant wives. Joseph is left out of this travel list because he was already established in Egypt. Naming each brother reminds readers that God cares for every individual family within His covenant people.

The whole company of Jacob's direct family came to seventy people, counting Joseph who was already in Egypt. God recorded this small starting number to show the wonder of what He did next. Over the next centuries, He multiplied this small band into a vast multitude.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that different ancient sources counted the group differently, with one source arriving at seventy without Jacob and others including him.

notes.meaning: As time passed, Joseph, all his brothers, and everyone of that first generation died. During their lifetimes, the Hebrews had enjoyed peace and high standing in Egypt. Their passing brought that safe era to an end and set the stage for a new test of faith.

The Israelites had many children, multiplying so fast that they seemed to swarm across the region of Goshen. They grew healthy, robust, and extraordinarily powerful. This rapid growth was the direct fulfillment of God's ancient promise to Abraham that his descendants would become as numerous as the stars.

A new king came to power in Egypt who had no personal knowledge of Joseph or his great achievements. He chose not to honor the debt of gratitude Egypt owed Joseph for saving the nation from famine. As a result, the Egyptian crown changed its policy from warm hospitality to suspicion.

The king gathered his officials and warned them that the Israelites were becoming too numerous and strong for Egypt. He argued that if war broke out, the Hebrews might join Egypt's enemies, fight against them, and leave the country. He used fear and political calculation to justify cruel measures against innocent neighbors.

The Egyptians appointed harsh taskmasters over the Israelites to break their spirits through crushing forced labor. Under this heavy burden, the Hebrews built the supply cities of Pithom and Rameses to store grain and wealth for Pharaoh. The king hoped exhausting labor would weaken their bodies, stop their growth, and kill their desire for freedom.

The harder the Egyptians worked the Israelites, the faster God caused them to increase and spread. Seeing them thrive despite every hardship filled the Egyptians with dread and loathing. Human cruelty could not overturn the blessing and purpose of God.

The Egyptians intensified their cruelty, forcing the Israelites into ruthless slavery. They made their everyday lives bitter with grueling work in clay, sun-dried brick, and heavy agricultural labor in the fields. Every task was enforced with harshness to break down their strength and dignity.

Pharaoh next launched a secret plot to wipe out Israel's future generations by speaking to Shiphrah and Puah, two leading midwives. He ordered them to inspect every baby on the delivery stool and kill all the boys while letting the girls live. By targeting only the newborn males, he hoped to slowly erase the Hebrew people without causing a sudden revolt.

The midwives feared God, holding deep reverence for Him and His law against taking innocent life. Because they dreaded God's displeasure more than the king's anger, they refused to carry out his murderous order. They chose to risk their own lives so the baby boys could live.

Pharaoh summoned the midwives back to his palace and demanded to know why they had spared the baby boys. He questioned their actions directly, putting them in immense personal danger. Despite facing the most powerful ruler of their day, the women stood firm in their allegiance to God.

The midwives told Pharaoh that Hebrew women were far hardier than Egyptian women and gave birth before a midwife could arrive. Hard outdoor labor had indeed made the Hebrew mothers strong, and God gave them remarkably swift deliveries. This answer satisfied the king's question and kept the children safe.

differ.view: Many in this tradition teach that the midwives told an untrue excuse, meaning that while their refusal to murder was holy, their deception was sinful and forgiven only by God's grace.
Some evangelicals hold that the midwives spoke the literal truth without lying, because the laboring Hebrew mothers truly experienced unusually quick births under God's special blessing.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that God rewarded the midwives for their mercy and fear of Him, but that their lie itself was a fault rather than a meritorious act.

notes.meaning: God responded with great kindness toward the midwives because they had honored Him and protected the helpless. In the meantime, the Israelite nation continued to multiply and became exceedingly mighty. Pharaoh's secret scheme had utterly failed to slow down God's work.

Because the midwives revered God and spared Israel's babies, He rewarded them by establishing families and households of their own. They had risked everything to protect the homes of God's people, and God repaid their kindness in kind. God never forgets the sacrifices made out of love for Him.

Having failed with his secret plots, Pharaoh abandoned all restraint and ordered open violence against the Hebrews. He commanded all Egyptian citizens to seize every newborn Hebrew boy and drown him in the Nile River, while sparing the baby girls. Even amid this terrible decree of death, God was already preparing a deliverer who would be drawn from that very river.
